title: An Essential Book for Teachers, Parents, and Anyone Interested in Learning
author: Jenna A. Robinson
summary: A review of Daniel Willingham's Why Don't Students Like School, arguing the cognitive-science classic should be assigned in every school of education. The review walks through Willingham's nine principles (e.g., 'factual knowledge must precede skills,' 'memory is the residue of thought'), praises the book's practical 'implications for the classroom' structure, but flags his thin treatment of what knowledge is actually worth teaching as a genuine weak point.
points: 75% of high school students report boredom, anger, sadness, fear, or stress in school, and suicidal ideation spikes during the school year versus breaks, per cited data.
Willingham's nine principles — including 'factual knowledge must precede skills' and 'memory is the residue of thought' — each get their own chapter with classroom implications.
The book challenges 'child-centered' orthodoxies, arguing learning-styles theory is overblown and that skills can't be taught in the absence of facts.
The reviewer's critique: Willingham's section on which knowledge to teach sidesteps the question, reframing it as 'whatever information writers assume readers know.'
Nearly a third of 12th-graders read at a 'below basic' level, per the review, framing the book's stakes as a matter of long-term societal health.
quotes: According to the American Institute of Stress, “75% of high school students report experiencing boredom, anger, sadness, fear, or stress in school.
In Why Don’t Students Like School, Willingham presents nine fundamental principles about how the mind works and what it means for teaching and learning.
Teaching, like any cognitive skill, must be practiced to be improved.
Willingham argues that students cannot simply be taught to think like experts.
Teachers are the single most important in-school factor affecting student achievement.
